discrepancies.quote: Either may recover some power, and a method that shares information between CpGs when it estimates the dispersion does not have the weakness of item 7.
discrepancies.problem: The item names Park and Wu 2016 as the DSS model "for designs with covariates" and then credits the option with sharing information between CpGs. Only the two-group model of DSS (Feng et al. 2014) does that. The general-design model of Park and Wu 2016, which is the one the draft's contrasts (ploidy with heat as covariate, heat with ploidy as covariate, the interaction) would need, estimates the dispersion CpG by CpG from a Pearson chi-squared statistic without shrinkage, bounds it at 0.001, and uses a normal reference distribution; its authors report a slightly inflated type I error with three replicates per group. The DSS functions for that model also return no methylation difference, so the draft's 20-point criterion cannot be applied inside DSS.
discrepancies.evidence: Park and Wu 2016, full text read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12157722/ ([S5]/text/park2016_PMC12157722.txt): the dispersion of each CpG is estimated from "Pearson χ2 statistics based on transformed linear model" and restricted "to be bounded by 0.001 and 0.999"; "The Wald test statistics approximately follow normal distribution"; "Under our setting, the EB-type of shrinkage method cannot be easily adopted because of the complicated relationship between the dispersion and data distribution"; Table 1 (type I error at 0.05; 3 and 10 replicates in each group of a 2 x 2 design): DSS-general 0.063 and 0.053, BiSeq 0.052 and 0.046, RADMeth 0.081 and 0.061, binomial GLM 0.151 and 0.175. DSS user's guide of DSS 2.60.0 (https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DSS/inst/doc/DSS.html, [S5]/text/DSS_vignette.txt): "for results from for multifactor design, {delta} is NOT supported". Feng et al. 2014 (PMC4005660): two-group comparison only; "in future work we plan to extend our model for two treatment groups to multifactor experimental designs". Lea, Tung and Zhou 2015 (PMC4657956): "methods based on beta-binomial models only account for over-dispersion due to independent variation, making them unsuited for data sets containing population structure or related individuals".
discrepancies.proposed_text: 3. Use a method built for replicated bisulfite data with few animals per group, or test regions instead of single CpGs. The two-group model of DSS is a beta-binomial model that shrinks the dispersion of each CpG towards a prior estimated from all CpGs (Feng, Conneely and Wu 2014, Nucleic Acids Res 42:e69, doi:10.1093/nar/gku154); it shares information between CpGs, does not have the weakness of item 7 and fits the ploidy contrast inside one cohort, but it takes no covariate. For a design with a covariate or an interaction DSS uses another model (Park and Wu 2016, cited in I-02), which estimates the dispersion CpG by CpG from a Pearson chi-squared statistic, without shrinkage, bounds it between 0.001 and 0.999 and refers a Wald statistic to the normal distribution. Its authors report a type I error of 0.063 at the 0.05 level with three replicates in each of four groups and 0.053 with ten (0.151 and 0.175 for a binomial model without overdispersion; their Table 1), and its functions return no methylation difference (DSS user's guide, version 2.60.0), so the 20-point criterion would have to be computed apart. For the draft's two contrasts and for the interaction that model is not shown to avoid the weakness of item 7. Beta-binomial models also take the animals of a group as independent; where relatedness among animals is aligned with the tested variable they give inflated statistics (Lea, Tung and Zhou 2015, PLoS Genet 11:e1005650, doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1005650; I-49). A test of regions (for example dmrseq, Korthauer et al. 2019, Biostatistics 20:367-383, doi:10.1093/biostatistics/kxy007) may recover some power. No method removes the confound of I-01 or the structure described in I-49, and any list should be checked against relabelled libraries in the same way.

discrepancies.where: 06_diagnostics/README.md, section "How to read the size of a list", paragraph after point 6 ("The analyses of this script are tests of single CpGs ...")
discrepancies.quote: Methods made for few animals share information between CpGs when they estimate that variation, or test regions (DSS: Feng, Conneely and Wu 2014, Nucleic Acids Res 42:e69, doi:10.1093/nar/gku154; dmrseq: Korthauer et al. 2019, Biostatistics 20:367-383, doi:10.1093/biostatistics/kxy007).
discrepancies.problem: Correct for the two-group model of DSS and for dmrseq, but a reader will take it to cover the draft's contrasts, which have a covariate. The DSS model for such designs (Park and Wu 2016) does not share information between CpGs.
discrepancies.evidence: Same sources as the entry on I-06, Options, item 3.
discrepancies.proposed_text: Methods made for few animals share information between CpGs when they estimate that variation (the two-group model of DSS: Feng, Conneely and Wu 2014, Nucleic Acids Res 42:e69, doi:10.1093/nar/gku154), or test regions (dmrseq: Korthauer et al. 2019, Biostatistics 20:367-383, doi:10.1093/biostatistics/kxy007). The model of DSS for designs with a covariate estimates the dispersion CpG by CpG, without sharing (Park and Wu 2016, Bioinformatics 32:1446-1453, doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btw026).

discrepancies.where: issues.md, I-08, paragraph "Why it matters" (text of 2026-11-18), first sentence
discrepancies.quote: In bisulfite data a C-to-T variant is indistinguishable from an unmethylated cytosine (Liu et al. 2012, Genome Biol 13:R61, doi:10.1186/gb-2012-13-7-r61).
discrepancies.problem: The cited paper says the opposite of "indistinguishable": its subject is that the reads of the opposite strand distinguish a C-to-T variant from bisulfite conversion. Only the reads of the strand that carries the cytosine cannot. The consequence drawn in I-08 stands, because Bismark does not look at variants, and the proposed resolution of I-08 (call variants from the alignments and mask them) relies on exactly this distinction.
discrepancies.evidence: Liu et al. 2012, full text from Europe PMC (PMC3491382; [S5]/text/liu2012_PMC3491382.txt): "This strand-specificity principle has been exploited in order to distinguish bisulfite conversion from C>T SNPs"; "approximately half the reads at a given cytosine position (those mapping to the 'C-strand') can be used for methylation quantification but cannot distinguish C>T SNPs. The other half (those mapping to the 'G-strand', boxed in Figure 1a) yield no methylation information but can be used to identify C>T SNPs." Venkataraman et al. 2022 (PMC9351233) on BS-Snper: "a thymine paired with an adenine indicates a C->T SNP, while a thymine paired with a guanine is a bisulfite-converted unmethylated cytosine" and "C->T single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) would be interpreted by Bismark as an unmethylated cytosine".
discrepancies.proposed_text: In the reads of the strand that carries the cytosine, a C-to-T variant cannot be told from an unmethylated cytosine, and Bismark counts it as unmethylated; the reads of the opposite strand show an A in place of a G and identify the variant, which is the principle of Bis-SNP (Liu et al. 2012, Genome Biol 13:R61, doi:10.1186/gb-2012-13-7-r61) and of the BS-Snper step of Venkataraman et al. 2022.

discrepancies.where: issues.md, I-02, paragraph "Why it matters" (text of 2026-11-18), last sentence
discrepancies.quote: Inferring an interaction from two separate significance calls is a known error (Gelman and Stern 2006, Am Stat 60:328, doi:10.1198/000313006X152649; Nieuwenhuis et al. 2011, Nat Neurosci 14:1105, doi:10.1038/nn.2886).
discrepancies.problem: Both papers describe another form of the error than the draft's: concluding that two effects differ because one is significant and the other is not. The draft's set requires two main effects (ploidy, heat) to be significant at the same CpG and compares no effects. The principle the papers state (a difference between effects must itself be tested) covers the draft's claim; the sentence as worded attributes to them an error they do not describe.
discrepancies.evidence: Nieuwenhuis et al. 2011, abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 21878926): "this comparison is often based on an incorrect procedure involving two separate tests in which researchers conclude that effects differ when one effect is significant (P < 0.05) but the other is not (P > 0.05)". Gelman and Stern 2006, abstract (OpenAlex record of the DOI): "changes in statistical significance are often not themselves statistically significant". Metadata of both verified at Crossref (Am Stat 60(4):328-331; Nat Neurosci 14(9):1105-1107).
discrepancies.proposed_text: A claim that an effect differs between groups needs a test of that difference, and separate significance calls do not provide one (Gelman and Stern 2006, Am Stat 60:328, doi:10.1198/000313006X152649; Nieuwenhuis et al. 2011, Nat Neurosci 14:1105, doi:10.1038/nn.2886, who describe the commonest form, one effect significant and the other not). The draft's set is further from such a test than that form: it requires two main effects to be significant at one CpG and compares no effects.

challenges.claim: I-06, correction paragraph, and header of 06_diagnostics/dml_sensitivity.R (note "Which of the two tests"), point 1: in the benchmark of Wreczycka et al. the default test without the correction had the lowest specificity and the best overall accuracy.
challenges.objection: The account was read by one agent in a preprint that nobody else could open; it might misstate the article, for example by taking the F-score of one data set for a general statement.
challenges.test_done: Read the published article in full (publisher's PDF from https://edoc.mdc-berlin.de/16722/; text in [S5]/text/wreczycka2017_mdc16722_raw.txt); located every statement on the default test in sections 4.1, 4.2 and 9; measured the bars of Figure 2 from the embedded image (scripts/measure_fig2_bars.py).
challenges.result: Confirmed in three places. Simulation (4.1): "MethylKit without overdispersion showed the lowest specificity (the overdispersion correction usually improves specificity)." Cell lines (4.2): "MethylKit without overdispersion had the highest F-score (Fig. 3c), but also the lowest specificity." and "it is still the best method when overall accuracy is considered". Conclusions (9): "has the best accuracy overall but highest false positive rate". Measured in Figure 2: specificity 0.68 to 0.71 for the default test (others 0.93 to 1.00); F-score 0.51 to 0.81 for the default test, the highest at every effect size (next: chi-squared with correction, 0.17 to 0.65).

challenges.claim: Same account, point 2: the F test with the correction gave results close to DSS.
challenges.objection: "Close to DSS" might hold for specificity only.
challenges.test_done: Same reading; Figure 2 measured.
challenges.result: Text (4.1): "F-test with overdispersion has similar results to DSS". Measured: specificity 0.98 to 0.99 (F test with correction) against 0.99 to 1.00 (DSS); sensitivity 0.02 to 0.10 against 0.00 to 0.39, so at effect sizes of 20 and 25 points DSS is the more sensitive of the two. The article's sentence is as the account gives it.

challenges.claim: Same account, point 3: the chi-squared test with the correction is named as a good compromise between stringent and relaxed methods.
challenges.objection: The article might recommend it outright (as the sentence of 2026-11-18 says) or not at all.
challenges.test_done: Same reading.
challenges.result: Stated twice as a compromise, once as an alternative: "We believe that a good compromise between the DSS/limma/F-test and default methylKit test is the overdispersion corrected methylKit Chi-square test." (4.1); "A good compromise between stringent and relaxed methods seems to be Chi-squared test with overdispersion correction." (4.2); "A good alternative to stringent and relaxed methods is Chi-square test after overdispersion correction (implemented in methylKit)." (9).

challenges.claim: Same account, point 4: the simulation had three samples per group.
challenges.objection: The number might be that of the real data.
challenges.test_done: Same reading.
challenges.result: "We simulated a dataset consisting of 6 samples (3 controls and 3 samples with treatment)." (4.1). The real data had two replicates per cell line: "ENCODE RRBS data (where each cell line has two replicates) for 19 human cell lines" (4.2).

challenges.claim: I-06, "Why it matters": the benchmark "shows a markedly higher false positive rate without the correction".
challenges.objection: The article prints no false positive rates; "markedly" may be the analyst's memory and not what the figure shows.
challenges.test_done: Measured the bar heights of Figure 2b (specificity) from the 300 dpi image embedded in the publisher's PDF, with the axis taken from the gridlines; checked the measurement through the identity between the three panels (F-score = F1 of precision and recall with 2,500 changed and 2,500 unchanged CpGs).
challenges.result: Share of unchanged CpGs called at q < 0.01 (1 minus specificity), by effect size 5 to 25: default test 29% to 32%; chi-squared with correction 5% to 7%; F with correction 1% to 2%; DSS 0.3% to 1.4%; limma 0.3% to 0.8%. The F-score panel is reproduced from panels a and b to within 0.006 at all 22 measurable bars (for example default test at 25 points: sensitivity 0.881, specificity 0.692, F1 0.805, measured 0.806). In the cell line data the text gives the same order without numbers. "Markedly" holds for the simulation: about 30% against 5% to 7% and 1% to 2%.

challenges.claim: I-06, "Why it matters": the benchmark "recommends `overdispersion = "MN"` with a chi-squared test".
challenges.objection: The methylKit authors may not recommend against their own default; an author could answer the audit with the article's statement that the default test is the best in overall accuracy.
challenges.test_done: Read sections 4.1, 4.2 and 9 for every recommendation; checked what "accuracy" is in the article.
challenges.result: The article recommends by purpose: default test "for more exploratory analysis"; limma, DSS and the F test with the correction "when there is a need to limit false positive rates, such as when picking regions or CpGs for validation"; chi-squared with the correction as "a good compromise". "Accuracy" is the F-score, which in Figure 2c equals the F1 score of precision and recall in a simulation where half of the CpGs are changed; the text defines it as the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity, which the plotted values do not match (default test at 25 points: 0.775 by that definition, 0.806 plotted). The benchmark contains no comparison of groups that do not differ, so its rating of the default test says nothing about the situation of items 2 and 5 of I-06.
challenges.proposed_text: See the replacement sentence and the replacement of the correction paragraph under discrepancies.

challenges.claim: I-06, item 4 (and README, result of the sensitivity analyses): the chi-squared form of the correction "does not hold its level"; "Its 14 and 185 CpGs are not a middle course between the two other columns."
challenges.objection: The methylKit authors' benchmark names exactly this test as the good compromise, so the log may be dismissing the recommended analysis on the strength of its own relabelling runs.
challenges.test_done: Derived from the measured Figure 2 what each test did to unchanged CpGs at the nominal q < 0.01 in the benchmark's own simulation (2,500 changed, 2,500 unchanged CpGs per effect size).
challenges.result: Chi-squared with correction: specificity 0.930 to 0.950, so 125 to 175 of 2,500 unchanged CpGs called; with its sensitivity of 0.10 to 0.51 that is a share of false calls among all calls of about 34% at 5 points falling to about 11% at 25 points, at a nominal 1%. Default test: about 39% to 26%. F with correction: about 33% to 10% (25 to 43 false calls; these small counts carry a reading error of about 8). DSS: about 8% to 3.5% at 15 to 25 points. The benchmark's "compromise" is one of sensitivity against specificity; its own figure shows that the chi-squared form called four to six times as many unchanged CpGs as the F form, which agrees with item 4 (7.2%, 2.2% and 0.47% of p-values below 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001 under relabelling). All values are pixel readings of a published figure and approximate.

challenges.claim: I-06, "What follows for the manuscript", first point: "The draft's settings are those of the methylKit vignette (default model, q < 0.01 and a difference threshold), so this is a finding about what common practice gives on these 22 libraries, not about an error of execution."
challenges.objection: Common practice in this laboratory may have been the corrected model: the paper whose Methods the draft's section 2.5 follows (I-28) might have used it.
challenges.test_done: Read the vignette of the installed methylKit 1.28.0 (methylKit.Rmd) and the Methods of Venkataraman et al. 2022 (BMC Genomics 23:556, full text from Europe PMC, PMC9351233; [S5]/text/venkataraman2022_PMC9351233.txt).
challenges.result: Vignette: `calculateDiffMeth(meth)` with defaults, then `getMethylDiff(myDiff,difference=25,qvalue=0.01)`; the statement on the vignette holds, with a 25-point threshold. Venkataraman et al. 2022: "A logistic regression (calculateDiffMeth) modeled the log odds ratio based on the proportion of methylation at each CpG locus. ... Additionally, an overdispersion correction with a chi-squared test (overdispersion = "MN", test = "Chisq") was applied."; DML "with at least a 50% methylation difference" that "did not overlap with C->T SNPs". The draft's Methods repeat the first of these sentences nearly word for word and omit the second; the draft's run had no correction, a 20-point threshold and no variant step. So the settings are those of the vignette, but not those of the paper the Methods are modelled on.
challenges.proposed_text: The draft's settings are those of the methylKit vignette (default model, q < 0.01 and a difference threshold, 25 points in the vignette), so this is a finding about what a common default gives on these 22 libraries. It is not the practice of the paper on which the draft's Methods 2.5 are modelled (I-28): Venkataraman et al. 2022 applied the correction with the chi-squared test, a 50% difference threshold and the removal of CpGs at C-to-T variants, and the draft's sentence on the model omits the correction.

challenges.claim: I-01, update, first point: "A uniform excess fits a difference in the conversion of mitochondrial DNA better than reads of another origin, which would be confined to the stretches they resemble; that is an inference, and the cause is not established."
challenges.objection: (a) The excess could be reads of nuclear copies of mitochondrial sequence, a variant, or real methylation at particular sites. (b) The published work on mitochondrial DNA in bisulfite data might not support incomplete conversion as the usual cause.
challenges.test_done: (a) Extracted the 363 mitochondrial rows of 04_output/05_differential_methylation/tables/united_cpg_legacy.csv.gz and computed, per library and per CpG, pooled percent methylation, the spread among CpGs against binomial sampling at one rate (Pearson chi-squared over degrees of freedom), and the share of the excess carried by the most extreme CpGs ([S5]/scripts/mito_cpg_check.R and mito_coverage_ratio.py; outputs in [S5]/mito/). (b) Read Liu et al. 2016, Mechta et al. 2017, Owa et al. 2018 (full texts), Hong et al. 2013 and Bicci et al. 2021 (abstracts).
challenges.result: (a) Every number of the paragraph is reproduced: 0.31% to 0.58% and 1.98% to 3.64%; cohort means 0.38% and 2.82%; control above heat at 363 of 363 CpGs; quartiles of the differences 1.64 and 3.14 points; coverage ratio 3.3 to 7.5 and 15.8 to 29.1. In addition: no CpG exceeds 5.95% in the control cohort (1.19% in the heat cohort); the ten CpGs with the largest excess carry 5.8% of the summed excess and the 36 largest 18.6%; without those 36 the cohort values are 0.395% and 2.585%. Among CpGs the control values are far more variable than binomial sampling at one rate gives (ratio 24.8) and the heat values are not (1.00). The heat-cohort rate equals the nuclear non-CpG rate (0.47% to 0.53%), the control rate is four to seven times it. (b) The literature attributes such signals to incomplete conversion of intact circular or supercoiled mitochondrial DNA, removed by linearization, with local unevenness (Liu 2016; Mechta 2017; Owa 2018). The inference stands and can be stated with sources.

challenges.claim: I-01, update ("the mitochondrial genome, a sequence expected to be unmethylated") and I-49, item 2 ("The 363 tested CpGs of the mitochondrial genome, which is expected to be unmethylated").
challenges.objection: The expectation comes from mammals and is contested even there; it may not hold for bivalves.
challenges.test_done: Searched Europe PMC for mitochondrial DNA methylation in molluscs and read the abstracts of the mammalian studies.
challenges.result: Mammals: absence, or values below 2% after linearization, in Hong et al. 2013, Liu et al. 2016, Mechta et al. 2017, Owa et al. 2018 and Bicci et al. 2021. Bivalves: one study, on gonads of Mytilus edulis, reports "the presence in mitochondria of methylated cytosines and adenines and methyltransferases" (Leroux et al. 2024). Nothing on oysters was found. In these data the heat libraries are at the level of nuclear non-CpG calls, which is what no methylation gives; the control libraries are not, and the literature offers incomplete conversion as the reason. As used in I-49, item 2, the mitochondrial rate measures the conversion of mitochondrial DNA, which in the control cohort is not that of nuclear DNA (2.0% to 3.6% against 0.5%), so there it is weak evidence about nuclear non-conversion.
challenges.proposed_text: In I-49, item 2, replace "which is expected to be unmethylated" by "which in mammals carries no CpG methylation or nearly none (sources in I-01; for bivalves the question is open)" and add after the parenthesis: "In the control cohort the mitochondrial rate is four to seven times the nuclear non-CpG rate, so it measures the conversion of mitochondrial DNA and not that of nuclear DNA (I-01); the comparison within cohort is not affected by this." The text for I-01 is under additions.

challenges.claim: I-49, item 2: "Neither incomplete bisulfite conversion nor the amount of sequencing explains the level." and "Whether the cause is biological ... or lies in library preparation cannot be decided from these data."
challenges.objection: The literature describes a technical cause that is neither of the two excluded: over-representation of methylated DNA through loss of unmethylated fragments during bisulfite treatment and through amplification, which raises the absolute level without raising non-conversion.
challenges.test_done: Read Olova et al. 2018 (full text) and Ji et al. 2014 (abstract) for the mechanism and for what it predicts; compared with the observations of item 2 and with the coverage ratio that check S2 computed (07_documentation/agent_workflows/verification_scripts/S2-I49-evidence-and-alternatives/02_alt1_artifacts.out; not recomputed by me).
challenges.result: Olova et al.: "depletion of unmethylated fragments, leading to an overestimation of the absolute 5mC values"; highly degrading conversion protocols "cause a direct 5-10% increase in the global estimate of DNA methylation"; "changes of up to 20% in DNA methylation can be purely technical". Ji et al.: enrichment for methylated DNA "is exacerbated by higher cycles of PCR". A selection of molecules by methylation state multiplies the odds of methylation at each CpG, which is the constant shift on the logit scale that item 2 reports, and leaves non-CpG calls nearly unchanged; item 2 does not exclude it. Both studies compared protocols; Olova et al. note that technical replicates of one technique gave few differences. In S2's output the ratio of coverage at methylated to unmethylated CpGs is unrelated to the level in the heat cohort (Spearman -0.27) and weakly related in the control cohort (0.57, p = 0.055), so the data give no positive sign of the mechanism either. The heading and the last sentence stand; the paragraph should name the mechanism and ask for the number of PCR cycles.

challenges.claim: I-49, item 2: "Methylation in CHH context, the usual measure of non-conversion".
challenges.objection: In a species with real non-CpG methylation the CHH rate would not measure non-conversion.
challenges.test_done: Read Wang et al. 2014 (abstract), Wreczycka et al. 2017 (section 3) and Lea et al. 2017 (full text).
challenges.result: C. gigas: "more than 99% methylation modification was restricted to cytosines in CpG context" (Wang et al. 2014). Practice: "For species without major non-CpG methylation, such as human, we can calibrate the conversion rate by using the percentage of non-CpG methylation ... typical values for a good experiment will be higher than 99.5%" (Wreczycka et al. 2017); the libraries here are at 99.5%. Lea et al. 2017 list CHH and CHG sites among the accepted estimators and add that spike-ins "seem to best capture a sample prep-related batch effect".

challenges.claim: I-49, "Why it matters": a response to heat confined to the diploids would produce the two differences; "so would five diploid animals that differed from the others before the treatment, or libraries that differ through their preparation."
challenges.objection: Differences between animals of one hatchery might be too small to matter beside a treatment, in which case the alternative would be a formality.
challenges.test_done: Searched Europe PMC and Crossref for family, genotype and sex effects on methylation in oysters; read abstracts and, where open, full texts.
challenges.result: Family: in 80 C. virginica of six full-sib families grown at two sites, "methylation patterns were largely driven by genetic differences among families", with "nearly a two orders of magnitude greater number of genes differentially methylated between families than between environments" (Johnson, Sirovy and Kelly 2022). C. gigas: parental methylated loci "stably transmitted to offspring" (Jiang et al. 2016); patterns "more similar between the two sires and their offspring" than between stages (Olson and Roberts 2014, preprint); "approximately half of the differentially methylated sites between the two parental strains were conserved in their offspring" (Teng et al. 2025). Sex: "females exhibiting a global reduction compared to males" in adductor muscle (Teng et al. 2025); male gonads more methylated (Sun, Li and Yu 2022); sex-specific methylation in gill of Ostrea edulis (Valk et al. 2025). The alternative is the better documented of the two in oysters; the one counter-example found is Johnson and Kelly 2020, where population-specific methylation was "not directly associated with single nucleotide polymorphisms".

challenges.claim: I-08, Evidence: "Diploid and triploid oysters in each cohort come from different crosses, and the two cohorts are different stocks (inference from the design; to be confirmed by the authors)." (repeated in I-01, update, third point: "come, by inference, from different crosses").
challenges.objection: Triploids can be made in eggs of the cross that gives the diploids, in which case the two ploidy groups of a cohort are full sibs; and the draft's Methods name one hatchery for all animals.
challenges.test_done: Read the FAO manual on triploid spat production (Vignier, Adams and Lovatelli 2024, full text), the abstracts of Miller et al. 2014 and 2016, and the Crossref record of Guo, DeBrosse and Allen 1996 (the article itself could not be opened).
challenges.result: Two methods exist. Mated triploids: "Sperm from tetraploid males (2n) is used to fertilise eggs from diploid females (1n)"; "Currently most hatcheries utilise the tetraploid approach ... however, in some places direct induction is used". A mated triploid has a tetraploid sire, so it cannot be a full sib of a diploid (the manual's cover shows "half-sibling diploid and triploid adult oysters"). An induced triploid comes from diploid parents and can be a full sib of diploids. "Different crosses" therefore holds if the triploids were mated triploids and is open otherwise; the method used for these animals is not recorded. Nothing in the literature bears on whether the two cohorts are different stocks.
challenges.proposed_text: Diploid and triploid oysters of a cohort come from different crosses if the triploids were made by mating tetraploid males with diploid females, the usual hatchery method (Guo, DeBrosse and Allen 1996, Aquaculture 142:149, doi:10.1016/0044-8486(95)01243-5; Vignier, Adams and Lovatelli 2024, FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper 698, doi:10.4060/cd1852en): such a triploid has a tetraploid sire and cannot be a full sib of a diploid. Triploids induced in eggs of a diploid cross can be full sibs of diploids. Which method was used, and whether the two cohorts are different stocks, is not recorded (inference from the design; to be confirmed by the authors).

challenges.claim: I-49, item 6: "A profile shared with animals of another experiment does not call for one cross or one processing batch among the triploids."
challenges.objection: If triploids are made from a tetraploid stock of little diversity, the triploids of both experiments could be related through their sires, and a shared profile would then be a family profile after all.
challenges.test_done: Read what the sources say about tetraploid stocks and parental contributions (Vignier et al. 2024; Miller et al. 2014, 2016) and set it against the observation of item 6.
challenges.result: The sources support relatedness among mated triploids: "the genetic diversity of tetraploids is generally limited" (Vignier et al. 2024); in two commercial triploid cohorts the effective population size was "34-49% lower than the census population" (Miller et al. 2016). But item 6 reports that the heat triploids resemble the control libraries of both ploidies (120 of 120 comparisons), and relatedness through tetraploid sires cannot make triploids resemble diploids of another experiment. The sentence stands. The sources bear on item 7 instead (complete separation of the heat triploids at 98 CpGs), which is what alleles from a common tetraploid sire line would give.

challenges.claim: I-01, "What is not affected": "The ELISA (N = 32) used the heat experiment's own control animals on one plate, so its heat effect is free of this confound".
challenges.objection: Free of the confound with experiment and sequencing batch, but the heat effect is then tested with animals as replicates. If the sixteen heat-treated animals were emersed together in one container and run, the treatment was applied once and the animals are subsamples of that application (pseudoreplication in the sense of Hurlbert 1984).
challenges.test_done: Read Hurlbert 1984 (abstract) and Lazic 2010 (full text); searched README.md, 03_input_files/metadata/README.md and 07_documentation/*.md for how the emersion was applied.
challenges.result: Hurlbert: pseudoreplication is testing "for treatment effects with data from experiments where either treatments are not replicated (though samples may be) or replicates are not statistically independent". Lazic: with a within-group correlation of 0.30 and ten per group a two-group test rejects 37% of the time at a nominal 5%. The repository records the treatment (24 h aerial emersion at 27 C) and not the number of containers or runs. The sentence holds as worded; whether the animals are independent replicates of the treatment cannot be tested from the repository.
challenges.proposed_text: Add to I-01, "Needs from authors": "Whether the 24 h emersion was applied to the heat-treated animals in one container and one run or in several, and how the control animals of that experiment were held meanwhile. If each treatment was applied once to one group of animals, the animals are subsamples of a single application of the treatment (Hurlbert 1984, Ecol Monogr 54:187, doi:10.2307/1942661), also for the ELISA (I-10)."

challenges.claim: I-49, "What would settle it": "Variant calls from the alignments (I-08); the same calls give the pairwise relatedness of the animals, which tests whether the triploids, or the diploids, of the heat experiment are one family without the pedigree."
challenges.objection: Genotypes called from bisulfite reads may be too error-prone for relatedness.
challenges.test_done: Read Lea et al. 2017 (full text) and Liu et al. 2012.
challenges.result: Supported with a caveat: "recent tools for calling SNP genotypes directly from BS reads (e.g., BisSNP and BS-SNPer) can help with constructing kinship/relatedness matrices, although not without error" (Lea et al. 2017; reference numbers removed from the quotation). Bis-SNP "correctly identified 96% of SNPs" at 30x coverage (Liu et al. 2012); the libraries here have a mean genome-wide coverage of 6 to 12 (column mean_cov_genome of 02_alt1_artifacts.out of check S2), and triploid genotypes add dosage classes.
challenges.proposed_text: Variant calls from the alignments (I-08); the same calls give an estimate of the pairwise relatedness of the animals, which tests whether the triploids, or the diploids, of the heat experiment are one family without the pedigree. Genotypes called from bisulfite reads carry error (Lea et al. 2017, cited in item 2), more so at the coverage of these libraries and in triploids, so the estimate separates full sibs from unrelated animals more safely than it grades relatedness.

challenges.claim: 06_diagnostics/README.md: "`share_of_labellings_at_least_observed` is a permutation p-value in which the observed labelling counts as one labelling (Phipson and Smyth 2010 ...)".
challenges.objection: The paper might recommend something else for randomly drawn permutations.
challenges.test_done: Read the abstract (Crossref and Europe PMC records).
challenges.result: The paper's point is that permutation p-values are "often computed incorrectly, understated by about 1/m, where m is the number of permutations" and that "permutation should be viewed as generating an exact discrete null distribution"; counting the observed labelling as one of the labellings is the correction it argues for. Metadata exact (Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol 9(1), Article 39).

challenges.claim: I-01, "Why it matters": "When a batch variable is perfectly aligned with the variable of interest, no statistical adjustment can separate them (Leek et al. 2010 ...)".
challenges.objection: The review might only recommend adjustment methods and not state this limit.
challenges.test_done: Read the author manuscript at PMC (PMC3880143; [S5]/text/leek2010_PMC3880143.txt).
challenges.result: "a confounded experiment will lead to incorrect biological conclusions because results due to batch will be impossible to distinguish from real biological effects"; "These approaches are most effective when batch effects are not highly confounded, or correlated, with the biological variables of interest." The sentence is a fair statement of the source.

additions.item: I-06: published statements on the uncorrected model that do not depend on the benchmark, and the practice of the paper the draft's Methods follow.
additions.why_it_matters: The first sentence of "Why it matters" carries the issue and now rests on one citation whose account was one-sided. Four independent sources state it directly, one of them with error rates for the same kind of design, and the methylKit paper itself says that the sample size is the number of reads. The paper on which the draft's Methods 2.5 are modelled applied the correction, which changes how the omission is to be read.
additions.where_to_add: issues.md, I-06, new paragraph directly after the paragraph "Correction to "Why it matters"".
additions.proposed_text: **What other published work says about the uncorrected model (2026-11-19).** The first sentence of "Why it matters" does not depend on that benchmark. The methylKit paper states that "the relevant sample sizes in logistic regression are not merely the number of biological samples but rather the total read coverages summed over all samples in each group separately" (Akalin et al. 2012, Genome Biol 13:R87, doi:10.1186/gb-2012-13-10-r87) and does not mention overdispersion. Taking reads of one animal as independent observations is pseudoreplication (Hurlbert 1984; Lazic 2010; both cited in I-49). In a simulation of a two by two design, a binomial regression without overdispersion had a type I error of 0.151 at the 0.05 level with three replicates per group and 0.175 with ten, which its authors call "not acceptable" (Park and Wu 2016, Table 1; cited in I-02). A guide for ecological studies calls binomial models "extremely false positive-prone" (Lea et al. 2017, cited in I-49), and pooling reads over replicates "ignores variation among biological replicates" (Feng, Conneely and Wu 2014, cited under Options). The paper on which the draft's Methods 2.5 are modelled (I-28) applied the correction: "an overdispersion correction with a chi-squared test (overdispersion = "MN", test = "Chisq") was applied", with a 50% difference threshold and after the removal of CpGs at C-to-T variants (Venkataraman et al. 2022, BMC Genomics 23:556, doi:10.1186/s12864-022-08781-5). The draft repeats that paper's sentence on the logistic regression and omits the one on the correction.

additions.item: I-01: published work on apparent methylation of mitochondrial DNA, and what the 363 CpGs show beyond the uniform excess.
additions.why_it_matters: The paragraph leaves the cause open as an inference. The literature names it (incomplete conversion of intact mitochondrial DNA, dependent on the state of the DNA and on the preparation), two further features of the data fit it, and without the sources a reader may take the sevenfold difference for an effect of heat on mitochondria, which the draft's Discussion would invite. "Expected to be unmethylated" also needs its source and its limit.
additions.where_to_add: issues.md, I-01, update of 2026-11-19, first point, directly after the sentence "A uniform excess fits a difference in the conversion of mitochondrial DNA better than reads of another origin, which would be confined to the stretches they resemble; that is an inference, and the cause is not established."
additions.proposed_text: Published work supports the inference. In mammals, where the question has been studied most, CpG methylation of mitochondrial DNA is absent or below 2% once the DNA is linearized before conversion, and higher values are an artifact: intact circular or supercoiled mitochondrial DNA resists bisulfite conversion, to an extent that differs between sample types and along the molecule (Hong et al. 2013, Mol Cell Biol 33:2683, doi:10.1128/MCB.00220-13; Liu et al. 2016, Sci Rep 6:23421, doi:10.1038/srep23421; Mechta et al. 2017, Front Genet 8:166, doi:10.3389/fgene.2017.00166; Owa et al. 2018, PLoS ONE 13:e0192722, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0192722). "Expected to be unmethylated" rests on that mammalian evidence; for bivalves one study reports methylated mitochondrial DNA in gonads of the mussel Mytilus edulis (Leroux et al. 2024, Sci Rep 14:31544, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-83368-6), so the expectation is not established for this species. Two more features of the data fit incomplete conversion. In the heat libraries the mitochondrial rate (0.31% to 0.58%) is at the level of nuclear non-CpG methylation (CHH 0.47% to 0.53% in all 22 libraries; `04_output/02_alignment_qc/tables/bismark_by_library.csv`), so their mitochondrial DNA was converted as completely as their nuclear DNA; in the control libraries it is four to seven times that level. And among the 363 CpGs the control values vary far more than sampling gives (Pearson chi-squared over degrees of freedom 24.8; largest value 5.95%), where the heat values vary as binomial sampling around one rate does (1.00); Owa et al. describe such local unevenness of conversion (`mito_cpg_check.out` in `07_documentation/agent_workflows/verification_scripts/S5-literature/`; computed once by the check of the citations, not yet written by a script of the repository). On this reading the two projects differ in the state of the DNA at conversion or in the conversion itself (extraction, fragmentation, denaturation, kit), none of which is recorded for the control libraries (I-36). It cannot be read as an effect of heat on mitochondrial DNA. Methylation at the non-CpG cytosines of the mitochondrial genome, which the alignments hold, would settle the cause: equal rates at CpG and non-CpG cytosines mean non-conversion.

additions.item: I-49, item 2: the technical and the biological causes of a raised overall level that the literature describes.
additions.why_it_matters: The item ends on "cannot be decided" without saying what the candidates are. One technical cause that the item's two checks do not exclude is documented (over-representation of methylated DNA), and one biological cause is documented for oysters and cannot be examined because it was not recorded (sex). Naming them makes the questions to the authors precise.
additions.where_to_add: issues.md, I-49, item 2, directly after its last sentence ("Whether the cause is biological ... cannot be decided from these data.").
additions.proposed_text: Published work gives candidates of both kinds. *Library preparation.* Fragments that carry unmethylated cytosines are lost preferentially during bisulfite treatment, and amplification builds on that loss, so that reads from methylated DNA are over-represented and the absolute level is overestimated by an amount that depends on the conversion protocol, the polymerase and the number of PCR cycles (Ji et al. 2014, Front Genet 5:341, doi:10.3389/fgene.2014.00341; Olova et al. 2018, Genome Biol 19:33, doi:10.1186/s13059-018-1408-2, who conclude that "changes of up to 20% in DNA methylation can be purely technical"). Such a bias multiplies the odds of methylation at every CpG, which is the constant shift on the logit scale described above, and it leaves the non-conversion rate unchanged, so the checks of this item do not exclude it. Both studies compared protocols; technical replicates of one protocol differed little in Olova et al., and no report of a difference of this size between libraries of one kit and one run was found. The efficiency of conversion can also differ between samples or groups of samples prepared together, and spike-in controls capture such batch effects better than non-CpG cytosines do (Lea et al. 2017, Nat Ecol Evol 1:1074, doi:10.1038/s41559-017-0229-0), which is the reason for asking for the values of the E. coli amplicons below. *The animal.* In adductor muscle of oysters, females have a globally lower methylation than males (Teng et al. 2025, Mar Biotechnol 27:31, doi:10.1007/s10126-024-10409-6); in C. gigas gonad the male is the more methylated sex (Sun, Li and Yu 2022, Gene 820:146260, doi:10.1016/j.gene.2022.146260); and gill tissue of the flat oyster Ostrea edulis carries sex-specific methylation (Valk et al. 2025, BMC Genomics 26:567, doi:10.1186/s12864-025-11736-1). The sample sheet (`03_input_files/metadata/wgbs_libraries.csv`) records no sex, so this cannot be examined. Methylation also follows family (see "Why it matters").

additions.item: I-49, "Why it matters": what published work says about family, ploidy, and the independence of animals, including how triploids are produced.
additions.why_it_matters: I-49 states the alternatives to a response to heat without a source. The literature on oysters makes one of them (family) the expected state of affairs, shows that earlier ploidy comparisons give no precedent for a ploidy difference in overall level in a somatic tissue, and explains why the triploids of an experiment are likely to be related through their sires without being one cross. This is what an author needs in order to answer the questions under "Needs from authors".
additions.where_to_add: issues.md, I-49, "Why it matters", as a new fourth point after the point on the ELISA.
additions.proposed_text: - What published work says about the alternatives. *Family.* In oysters methylation follows family more than environment: among 80 eastern oysters (Crassostrea virginica) of six full-sib families grown at two sites, methylation patterns "were largely driven by genetic differences among families", with nearly two orders of magnitude more genes differentially methylated between families than between sites (Johnson, Sirovy and Kelly 2022, J Anim Ecol 91:1135, doi:10.1111/1365-2656.13645). In C. gigas methylation patterns are transmitted from parents to offspring and differ between families (Jiang et al. 2016, Mar Biotechnol 18:124, doi:10.1007/s10126-015-9674-4; Olson and Roberts 2014, bioRxiv, doi:10.1101/012831, a preprint; Teng et al. 2025, cited in item 2), and in the Olympia oyster pairwise methylation distance correlates with genetic distance (Pearson 0.27; Silliman et al. 2023, Genome Biol Evol 15:evad013, doi:10.1093/gbe/evad013). Two groups of animals from different crosses are therefore expected to differ at many CpGs whatever their ploidy or treatment. *Ploidy.* The two published comparisons of diploid and triploid C. gigas report no difference in the global level (methylation-sensitive amplified polymorphism; Jiang et al. 2016) and, in gonad, a decreased CpG methylation level in infertile triploids and the opposite in fertile ones (WGBS; Sun, Yu and Li 2022, Mar Biotechnol 24:18, doi:10.1007/s10126-021-10083-y). Neither is on ctenidium or on a response to heat, and no comparison in another bivalve was found; they give no precedent for a ploidy difference in overall level in a somatic tissue. *Independence.* Animals of one cross, or animals treated together in one container, are not independent replicates of a ploidy or of a treatment (Hurlbert 1984, Ecol Monogr 54:187, doi:10.2307/1942661; Lazic 2010, BMC Neurosci 11:5, doi:10.1186/1471-2202-11-5; Lazic and Essioux 2013, BMC Neurosci 14:37, doi:10.1186/1471-2202-14-37, for litters), and in bisulfite data relatedness that is aligned with the tested variable gives spurious associations (Lea, Tung and Zhou 2015, cited in I-06; Lea et al. 2017, cited in item 2). Triploids for aquaculture are mostly made by mating tetraploid males with diploid females (Guo, DeBrosse and Allen 1996, Aquaculture 142:149, doi:10.1016/0044-8486(95)01243-5; Vignier, Adams and Lovatelli 2024, FAO Fisheries and Aquaculture Technical Paper 698, doi:10.4060/cd1852en). Two of the three chromosome sets of such a triploid come from a tetraploid stock whose genetic diversity "is generally limited" (Vignier et al. 2024; Miller et al. 2014, Aquaculture 433:318, doi:10.1016/j.aquaculture.2014.06.025), and a mated triploid cannot be a full sib of a diploid. Commercial triploid cohorts are mostly made by mass spawning of several parents, not as one cross, but the parents contribute unequally: in two such cohorts the effective population size was 34% to 49% below the census number (Miller et al. 2016, Aquac Res 47:1288, doi:10.1111/are.12588). How the triploids of the two experiments were made is not recorded.

additions.item: I-49, "Needs from authors": four questions that follow from the literature.
additions.why_it_matters: The present list asks for source, crosses, batches and records of seven animals. The sources show that four more facts decide between the alternatives: how the triploids were produced and from how many parents, the sex of all 22 animals, the preparation details that set the absolute level (kit and conversion protocol of project zr3644, number of PCR cycles), and whether the treatment was applied to one group of animals at once.
additions.where_to_add: issues.md, I-49, "Needs from authors": the first text is appended to the first point; the three others are new points before the last one.
additions.proposed_text:
(appended to the first point) How were the triploids of each experiment produced: by mating tetraploid males with diploid females, or by induction in eggs of the cross that gave the diploids? How many sires and dams contributed to each of the four groups?
- The sex of all 22 animals, if it was recorded or can be read from histology (item 2).
- For both projects: the method of DNA extraction, the amount of DNA that went into each library, the library kit and bisulfite conversion protocol, and the number of PCR cycles of each library. The sample sheet records the kit for the heat libraries only (`03_input_files/metadata/wgbs_libraries.csv`, column `library_kit`); absolute methylation levels depend on the conversion protocol, the polymerase and the number of cycles (item 2), and the conversion of mitochondrial DNA differs between the two projects (I-01).
- Whether the 24 h emersion was applied to the heat-treated animals in one container and one run or in several, and how the control animals of that experiment were held meanwhile. If each treatment was applied once to one group of animals, the animals are subsamples of a single application of the treatment (Hurlbert 1984, cited under "Why it matters"), also for the ELISA (I-01, I-10).

additions.item: I-08: how often C-to-T variants produced candidate DML in C. gigas in the study whose methods the draft follows, and the one result that points the other way.
additions.why_it_matters: I-08 argues from principle. A number exists for this species, tissue type aside, with the same laboratory's pipeline: one candidate DML in five overlapped a C-to-T variant among siblings. It turns "can appear as DML" into an expected share and supports the proposed resolution.
additions.where_to_add: issues.md, I-08, new paragraph after "Why it matters" (before "Proposed resolution").
additions.proposed_text: **What published work adds (2026-11-19).** How often this happens in this species is on record. In the WGBS study of C. gigas gonad on which the draft's Methods are modelled (I-28), 315 of 1,599 candidate DML (19.7%) overlapped C-to-T variants called from the same reads and were removed, "even though specimens were sibling oysters with similar genomic backgrounds" (Venkataraman et al. 2022, BMC Genomics 23:556, doi:10.1186/s12864-022-08781-5; eight animals, 50% difference threshold). Unless the animals compared here are as closely related as siblings, the share is not expected to be smaller. Besides variants at the CpG itself, methylation follows genotype through variants elsewhere (I-49, "Why it matters"). One result points the other way: in Olympia oysters, variants that create or remove a CpG were only slightly more frequent near DML than other variants (0.9% against 0.4% within 350 bp), with sparse genotyping (Silliman et al. 2023, Genome Biol Evol 15:evad013, doi:10.1093/gbe/evad013).

citations.excerpt: MethylKit without overdispersion showed the lowest specificity (the overdispersion correction usually improves specificity). F-test with overdispersion has similar results to DSS, whereas the Chi-squared test with overdispersion correction has similar specificity to stringent methods such as DSS and limma but achieves higher sensitivity (Fig. 2c). Overall, DSS and limma are not very sensitive but very specific. We believe that a good compromise between the DSS/limma/F-test and default methylKit test is the overdispersion corrected methylKit Chi-square test.
citations.note: Supports "higher false positive rate without the correction" (measured from Figure 2b: about 30% of unchanged CpGs called by the default test, 5% to 7% by the chi-squared test with the correction, 1% to 2% by the F test with the correction). Does not support "recommends" as worded: the chi-squared test with the correction is a compromise, the default test is rated best in overall accuracy and accepted for exploratory analysis. Page range 105-115. The text defines the F-score as the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity; the plotted values are the F1 score of precision and recall at 50% changed CpGs.

(1) At NC_047565.1:35,030,701 and the CpG 16 bp away, the five heat-cohort triploids have 11/24, 12/32, 10/24, 11/31 and 10/16 methylated reads, and 13/24, 14/33, 13/28, 11/32 and 16/20; that is four animals between 34% and 54% (40% and 44% with their reads pooled) and one at 62% and 80%.
